newsitem.title: USA: Aetna profits drop, stock tumbles.
newsitem.headline: Aetna profits drop, stock tumbles.

text.p: Aetna Inc., one of the nation's biggest health insurance companies, posted second-quarter profits that disappointed investors Tuesday and scaled back its growth projections for the year.
Investors drove its stock down more than 10 percent.

Aetna said net income fell 20 percent to $230 million in the quarter from $288 million a year earlier. Excluding charges due mainly from writing off intangible assets, the company earned $1.27 a share, down from $1.43 a share.

Although the per-share figures were in line with Wall Street estimates, the results were overshadowed by a downturn in operating earnings in parts of Aetna's health insurance business from the first quarter, analysts said.

In addition, the company's decision to post $31 million from its reserve fund toward the current quarter's profits inflated earnings by about 12 cents a share, said Smith Barney analyst Geoffrey Harris.
Citing a disappointing performance by the company's managed-care business, Harris lowered his rating on Aetna's stock to "outperform" from "buy."

Aetna said it was trimming the outlook for health maintenance organisation and Medicare enrollment growth to about 10 percent this year from about 14 percent as it has resisted cutting prices to attract business.
Commercial HMO enrollment grew 10 percent in the second quarter, but that fell short of analysts' expectations.
The Hartford, Conn.-based company's second-quarter health insurance results also were hurt by an increase in commercial HMO and Medicare medical costs, analysts said.
"Medical costs were a little higher, pricing was at the low end of prior indications and enrollment was at the low end," Salomon analyst Robert Hoehn said.

"The most important thing is that they reduced their growth outlook in terms of membership growth for the HMOs," Nutmeg Securities analyst Ira Zuckerman said. "The biggest thing is concern about the growth outlook. This is supposed to be a growth stock in a growth business."
Aetna stock tumbled $14.25 to $102.75 in consolidated New York Stock Exchange trading. It was one of the most active issues.

Operating profits in Aetna's health risk segment -- where the company assumes all or a majority of health care costs and risk -- fell to $172 million in the quarter from $198 million in the first quarter of 1997.
The company said higher commercial and Medicare costs more than offset higher premium rates.
Aetna merged with managed care company U.S. Healthcare in July of last year. Fuelled by the merger, revenues climbed to $4.6 billion from $3.2 billion.
Separately, Oxford Health Plans Inc. said net income surged 66 percent in the quarter, driven by increased enrollment and stable medical costs.
The Norwalk, Conn.-based health insurer said its profits climbed to $37 million in the second quarter from $22.5 million a year ago.
Earnings per share jumped to 45 cents from 28 cents a year ago and beating analysts' average estimate by one cent.

But the strong results were not enough to insulate the company's stock from an industry-wide sell-off, and Oxford fell $3.6875 to $82.125 on Nasdaq, as jitters tied to Aetna's results spread to other managed care stocks.
"Apparently, the Aetna downgrade (by Smith Barney) was disappointing to investors and Oxford fell off in sympathy," said PaineWebber health care analyst David Lothson.
Revenues reached $1.06 billion for the quarter ended June 30, a 46 percent increase from $725.3 million a year ago.
Oxford also announced that its founder, Stephen Wiggins, had resigned as chief executive but will remain as chairman. Acting CEO William Sullivan was named to the spot.
Oxford markets health insurance plans to employers in New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Connecticut and New Hampshire.
